insider_note: x is exactly half of 2x, and 2x is the derivative of x²+16 — spotting that pairing turns an apparently hard square-root integral into a one-line substitution.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write x dx as half of d(x²+16)
steps.margin_note: First mark. ∫f'(x)dx/√f(x) = 2√f(x) — recognise the numerator as half the derivative of the expression under the root.
steps.memory_tip: x is half of 2x, and 2x is exactly d(x²+16)/dx — recognise that pairing first.
steps.why: x dx is exactly half the derivative of x²+16 (which is 2x dx), so multiplying and dividing by 2 turns the integral into the standard form ∫f'(x)dx/√f(x), whose antiderivative is 2√f(x).
common_mistakes: Treating x dx as the derivative of x²+16 without the missing factor 2.
Forgetting to halve the result after inserting the factor 2.

steps.label: Apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both √25 and √16 are perfect squares — check the arithmetic lands on whole numbers.
steps.memory_tip: At x=0 the x² term vanishes, leaving only the constant under the root.
steps.why: Substituting x=3 gives √25=5 and x=0 gives √16=4; the difference is the value of the definite integral.
common_mistakes: Missing the +16 term when x=0, giving √0 instead of √16.
